news.title: Jon Ossoff's 2028 Chances Get Boost as Harris and Newsom Dip—New Poll
news.text: Senator Jon Ossoff is gaining ground in early polling of the potential 2028 Democratic presidential field, as support for former Vice President Kamala Harris and California Governor Gavin Newsom has slipped from earlier highs. Candidates typically begin announcing their runs after the midterms, though it’s not unprecedented for candidates to jump in even before those elections. No candidate in the poll has formally entered the 2028 presidential race. Although Ossoff has previously indicated that he has "zero interest" in running for president in 2028, and regardless of the fact that the poll places him well behind the Democratic frontrunners at 7 percent, Morning Consult singled him out as “the mover” in the field after his support more than doubled from 3 percent in the previous polling wave. He has climbed from just 1 percent in May and is the only Democrat to post gains in three consecutive waves. Harris remains the clear leader in the hypothetical Democratic primary field with 24 percent support, followed by Newsom at 12 percent and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 9 percent. Morning Consult surveyed 2,203 registered voters from August 28-30, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2 percentage points. The 2028 primary results reflect responses from voters in each party’s respective primary. Morning Consult described the Democratic race as “quieter on top and busier underneath.” Harris has remained unchanged across the last five polling waves, while Newsom has slid from 19 percent in June to his weakest point so far this year. Ossoff, meanwhile, has continued to gain. Newsweek has reached out to Ossoff’s campaign for comment. Patrick Casale, senior adviser to Nevada GOP Chairman Michael McDonald, told Newsweek that Ossoff’s path to becoming a serious 2028 presidential contender could depend on how the Democratic Party’s socialist wing performs in the midterms. If Democratic socialist candidates perform well, he predicted the party would push Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for president. But “if they lose in the midterms, they’re not going to run with her [AOC],” Casale said. “That’s where Ossoff’s numbers are going to work.” Casale said he was not surprised by Newsom and Harris’ polling numbers. “California is totally destroyed. He’s [Newsom has] destroyed paradise. He’s ruined paradise. And where’s Harris from? Oh, that would be California,” Casale said. What Is Driving Attention Around Jon Ossoff? Ossoff’s polling gains come as the Georgia senator has drawn increasing national attention in recent weeks, including for his more confrontational approach toward President Donald Trump and his administration. During an August rally, Ossoff threw Trump aide Natalie Harp into the spotlight while criticizing the president’s priorities and handling of the Iran war. “He doesn’t want to do the job,” Ossoff said of Trump. “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie.” Asked about Ossoff’s remarks the following day, Trump again compared the Georgia senator to Pee-wee Herman, calling him a “Pee-wee Herman lookalike” before adding: “No, I would much rather do other things.” Ossoff later leaned into the reaction, telling MS NOW it had been “amazing” to watch the White House “melt down” over his remarks. What Other 2028 Polls Show Other recent polling has also placed Harris at the front of the potential 2028 Democratic field, though the size of her lead has varied considerably. A Rasmussen Reports poll released earlier in August found Harris with 37 percent support among likely Democratic primary voters, putting her well ahead of Newsom, who received 14 percent. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York followed at 9 percent, while former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg received 8 percent. The Rasmussen poll was conducted from July 15 to July 21 among 472 respondents. An Emerson College poll conducted in July painted a different picture, with Buttigieg leading at 19 percent and Newsom at 17 percent. Ossoff and Ocasio-Cortez each received 13 percent, while Harris stood at 8 percent. Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear received 7 percent, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro 5 percent and Illinois Governor JB Pritzker 3 percent. Representative Ro Khanna received 2 percent, while 3 percent chose someone else and 13 percent were undecided. The poll was conducted from July 19 to July 20 among 574 respondents and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The Rasmussen and Emerson College polls paint markedly different pictures of the potential Democratic field, largely because of Harris' standing. What Does the Poll Show About the 2028 Republican Field? The Morning Consult polling also found movement in the potential Republican presidential field, particularly for Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Rubio received 22 percent support in the August poll, an increase of 7 percentage points from July. Morning Consult described the increase as the “first real movement in the Republican field since March” and said the jump exceeded the survey’s margin of error. Vice President JD Vance remained the clear Republican front-runner with 36 percent support. However, Morning Consult noted that the figure was Vance’s lowest level in the polling so far and that his lead was less than half the 33-point advantage he held in March. Rubio was also the only Republican other than Vance to reach double-digit support in any of Morning Consult’s polling waves. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis received 8 percent support, while Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. stood at 5 percent. Morning Consult said neither had moved outside the poll’s margin of error. No candidate in the poll has formally entered the 2028 presidential race, and while Ossoff says he has "zero interest" in the position, Harris said she was "thinking" about it, AOC said her goal is to "change the world", and Newsom left it to "fate." news.title: Grammy Winner Calls Out Singers Chasing Dolly Parton’s Country Crown
news.text:
Dolly Parton has never been just the Queen of Country Music. For an artist of her reach, even that crown feels too small for her five-foot frame.

She can command the Grand Ole Opry one moment and share a Hollywood soundstage with Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin the next. She wrote the songs, starred in the films, built the businesses, donated millions of books, created a theme park empire and turned towering wigs into part of an instantly recognizable brand.

Parton is rarer than a superstar: she is a public figure almost everyone seems willing to embrace. In America, that alone borders on miraculous.

That enduring affection is the real legacy of the Smoky Mountain Songbird, who remains one of country music’s most beloved and commercially powerful figures at 80.

But can anyone really stand in Dolly’s place?

Music industry insiders say Nashville is already buzzing with debate, as teams behind established names and rising contenders position their stars for the next era of country dominance.

Shania Twain helped push country beyond its old borders. Carrie Underwood has the powerhouse voice. Miranda Lambert carries deep genre credibility. Ella Langley has the momentum of a breakout. Still, many who know the business argue that none of them can match the full force of Parton’s cultural impact.

One obvious answer is Taylor Swift.

She began as a teenage Nashville songwriter. Country became country-pop, then pop, then stadium culture. Much like Parton, Swift stopped belonging to a genre long ago.

On paper, Swift has everything it takes to fill Parton’s boots: country roots, songwriting credibility, business instincts, crossover appeal and global fame.

‘Taylor is the only woman alive who comes close to Dolly’s combination of songwriting, business power and global reach,’ a veteran Nashville executive tells me before adding the cutting caveat: ‘But Dolly made people forget their politics. Taylor brings politics into the room.’

Swift endorsed Kamala Harris in 2024 and has made no secret of her disdain for Donald Trump. So, Swift can kiss her Dolly crown goodbye.

Parton understood something almost no celebrity grasps anymore: Why opine on politics and risk alienating half your audience?

She spent decades refusing to become property of either tribe, declining the Presidential Medal of Freedom three times: twice from Trump, for personal and Covid-related reasons, and later from Joe Biden because she worried accepting it after rejecting Trump would look partisan.

As Parton put it: ‘I learned a long time ago, keep your damn mouth shut if you want to stay in show business… I’m not in politics, I’m an entertainer.’

Beyoncé belongs in the conversation, too.

Her country turn reinforced something Parton proved for decades: genres get more interesting when somebody opens the doors. Cowboy Carter made history, the supporting tour grossed over $400 million, making it the highest-grossing country roadshow ever, and the record itself won Best Country Album and Album of the Year at the 2025 Grammy Awards.

But Nashville power players don’t see her ability to sustain a presence.

‘Let’s stop pretending Cowboy Carter was some flawless country masterpiece,’ one Grammy award winner tells me. ‘I thought the album was wildly overrated. And that Jolene cover? A complete misfire. Dolly’s original is heartbreaking because it’s vulnerable — Beyoncé turned it into a threat. That completely misses what makes the song so devastating.’

The source adds that Beyoncé’s enormous talent isn’t the issue:

‘Beyoncé is one of the greatest performers alive. But the doesn’t mean you’re automatically great at country music. Nashville was terrified to say that out loud because nobody wanted to be accused of having some ulterior motive.’

There are a few other honorable mentions.

Reba McEntire is royalty: funny, warm and adored across generations.

‘Reba has the affection, credibility and humor,’ a country insider tells me. ‘But Dolly escaped country. She belonged to people who didn’t even know they liked country music.’

Grandmothers, gay men, church ladies, drag queens, conservatives, liberals, children and movie stars loved Parton. She achieved celebrity’s rarest trick: broad affection without becoming bland.

MORE STORY: Pete Hegseth Faces Pentagon Revolt as Generals Break Ranks

Lainey Wilson may have the most interesting future because she has something increasingly rare: authenticity.

‘Lainey has what Dolly had early,’ a Nashville manager tells me. ‘Within thirty seconds, you know exactly who she is. The problem is scale.’

Wilson, I’m told, is thought to lack the outsized personality to sit in Parton’s throne.

‘Ella Langley is having a moment, but moments come and go. I’m not convinced she has the staying power to still matter 30 years from now,’ my Grammy-winning source says.

‘Kacey Musgraves has the talent, the Grammys and the credibility, but she doesn’t have Dolly’s universal connection,’ they added.

‘Kacey is cool and critically adored, but Dolly was never just cool — she was loved. There’s a huge difference. That kind of connection can’t be manufactured, marketed or won at the Grammys.’

Then there is Miley Cyrus.

If Swift is Dolly’s commercial heir, Cyrus may be her emotional one.

Parton was her godmother, and their relationship was real and lasting. Cyrus also has the crossover gene: country, rock, pop and blues all fit her.

‘Miley inherited Dolly’s fearlessness more than anyone,’ a music-industry source tells me. ‘Dolly controlled the joke before anyone could use it against her. Miley learned the same lesson: if people are going to talk, give them something worth talking about.’

Same survival instinct. Different bra.

In the end, however, true Music City insiders say all these divas may be spinning their wheels in the country mud.

‘Everybody keeps asking who the next Dolly is,’ a longtime entertainment executive tells me. ‘There isn’t one. The talent exists. The culture that created her doesn’t.’

That is the real story. Broadcasting is dying – not just television or radio, but cultural broadcasting itself. We once watched the same shows, heard the same stations and knew the same stars. Now algorithms determine our viewing habits.

Your TikTok is different from mine. Your Spotify makes different suggestions. Your Netflix home screen looks like we live on different planets.

‘A celebrity can have 20 million followers and still be invisible to half the country,’ a top music booker tells me. ‘We don’t manufacture universal stars anymore because we don’t have a universal culture anymore.’

Swift may be bigger commercially. Cyrus may be more wild. Wilson may become country’s next great star. McEntire may remain its beloved grande dame.

But another Parton?

Honey, good luck.

Leave the crown exactly where she left it: empty, impossible to inherit and encrusted in rhinestones.

news.title: 'I was duped': 3-time Trump voter fumes at 'glorified snake oil salesman'
news.text:
A self-described "3-time Trump voter" complained on Twitter that she is upset with President Donald Trump's policies — but also refused to admit she voted wrong in the 2024 election.

"I say this as a 3-time Trump voter, a lifelong Republican who spent an embarrassing amount of money on merch and travel to Trump rallies and DC," Lucy Riles posted on X. "I was duped. The past 14 months have been betrayal after betrayal. It sucks admitting I got it wrong. No, I’m not saying Kamala [Harris] would have been better. But Trump is a politician, a glorified snake oil salesman. He is not God nor should he be worshiped as one. And we need to hold our politicians accountable. Especially the ones we voted for and sacrificed friendships, jobs and family over."

Riles added, "Trump is now attempting to bully his base into supporting another reckless foreign war, ignore the Epstein files and now, accept data centers or else you want to be 'backwards and poor.' I’ve never been in an emotionally abusive relationship[,] and I’m not about to start now."

She concluded, "Thank you for your attention to this matter."

Earlier in August, a separate three-time Trump voter complained on MS NOW that even though the president promised to reduce inflation once in office, "the prices haven't gone down. I don't know, I'm just, I'm over it, I think, over the Trump thing, the Trump wagon — whatever you want to call it."

Another Trump voter griped, “It's hard. It makes me feel like I'm a horrible mother sometimes because I'm stressing about what I'm going to do — do I have enough money to put gas in, or do I need to buy eggs and milk for my child? Or do I need to not go to work every day to make that money because gas prices are so expensive?”

That voter concluded, “And mind you, it could be my fault — I do work in cleaning, but still, that's a 45-minute drive. We're putting 80 bucks in every three days, tops, maybe. It's just hard to feel good when everything's going downhill, I feel like. It's supposed to be going up, and sometimes, yes, it is up, and then all of a sudden it just goes down. And then we're always told, you know, ‘this is going to change’ or ‘I'm going to make this better’ or ‘we're going to make this better’ — but where's it at? We're not seeing it at all.”

Also earlier in August, a Trump voter and Iowan named Stephen Foot observed to MS NOW that "the prices haven't gone down. I don't know, I'm just, I'm over it, I think, over the Trump thing, the Trump wagon — whatever you want to call it." Still another Trump voter proclaimed earlier in August that, regarding the war in Iran, “Enough! Bring our guys and girls home. I don't want to see it — I don't like seeing war, that's all. We need to protect our borders and keep our family here safe.”

More recently, and also on Monday, former MAGA lawmaker ex-Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-GA) accused Trump of "disloyalty" to his own base.

"I hear this from people literally every single day," Greene posted on X. "There is absolutely nothing wrong with saying this and demanding your elected leaders deliver exactly what they promised you when you voted, donated, and supported them. The disloyalty comes from Trump, not people like this."

news.title: Tensions erupt in House hearing as GOP advances anti-socialism resolution while Dems rage: 'Silly season'
news.text: House Republicans are teeing up a pair of bills this week to put Democrats on the record about where they stand on their party's socialist insurgency. The House Rules Committee just advanced a resolution to condemn socialism during its Monday meeting, with no Democrats voting in favor of moving it forward. Democrats, in fact, criticized the resolution as a waste of time. Rep. Jim McGovern, D-Mass., called the bill "nonsense" and argued it did little to better the lives of Americans. "So you're concerned about rising gas, or are you concerned about grocery prices? You know, don't worry. Republicans in Congress are passing another non-binding resolution condemning socialism," McGovern said. HOUSE REPUBLICAN AIMS TO PUT DEMOCRATS ON THE RECORD OVER DSA WITH RESOLUTION CONDEMNING SOCIALISM Tensions erupted at one point as Rep. Joe Neguse, D-Colo., clashed with Committee on House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis., over the definition of socialism. Neguse had attempted to press Steil on whether he would see President Donald Trump trying to take a "20% stake" in Kroger grocery stores as socialism, to which Steil replied he would "want to see the details." "Oh, you'd want to see the details," Neguse yelled as the two men spoke over each other. "You said if the government owns grocery stores, that would be socialist. But if, of course, Donald Trump were to announce an equity stake in a grocery store, well, 'I'd have to really see the details,' because we all know the play." Steil said he would be open to seeing such a proposal if it had a national security imperative, but stated repeatedly that Neguse was posing a hypothetical. At one point, Rules Committee Chairwoman Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., chided Neguse for interrupting Steil. Steil shot back at one point, "Some folks on your side of the aisle would like to have government-run grocery stores. I think that's nuts." "And if the president of the United States announced that the United States government was taking an...equity stake in grocery stores?" Neguse pressed. After more back-and-forth, Steil said, "I think there would need to be a national security rationale for the action. I don't see any in your hypothetical. I don't see a national security focus." Neguse called it a "helpful answer," to which Steil quipped, "It's a hypotherical. So we're entering silly season." A House-wide test known as a "rule vote" on the resolution will take place on Tuesday afternoon, followed finally by a vote on the resolution itself on Tuesday evening, according to a provisional schedule obtained by Fox News Digital. SOCIALISM SURGES AMONG DEMOCRATS AS PARTY LEADERS REJECT DSA AGENDA: ‘PACK OF FOOLS’ It's not uncommon for Democrats on the House Rules Committee to oppose GOP-led measures. But the move is especially stark as Republicans seize on the left's inter-party civil war that has dominated the midterm election cycle. Republicans are capitalizing on that civil war with another measure expected for a vote on Wednesday afternoon, according to that provisional schedule. That vote will be on a constitutional amendment to cap the number of Supreme Court justices at nine. DEMOCRATIC SENATOR CLAIMS GOP 'STOLE' TWO SCOTUS SEATS IN 2016, 2020, CALLS FOR EXPANSION Several top progressives, including former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Ed Markey, D-Mass., have called for expanding the Supreme Court to up to 13 seats. House GOP leaders have opted to fast-track that legislation past the House Rules Committee. In exchange, however, it will need two-thirds of the chamber to pass as opposed to a simple majority. CARVILLE UNLOADS ON DSA SOCIALISTS: 'DON'T USE OUR GOD---- NAME' "It's time for the Democrats to pick a side. Stop playing the middle. Be proud of who you are. You were elected to lead, so lead. Have an opinion. We intend to put you on record," House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain, R-Mich., told Fox News Digital. "Do you want to pack the Supreme Court or not? It's really simple. It's a yes or no vote. It's no bigger than that. Two — do you believe in socialism? If you do, you should say it loud and say it proud. I personally don't believe in socialism. I like the fact that we have a democracy, that we have a republic, that we have a free society. And I'm proud to put myself on record." Meanwhile the top Democrat, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., side-stepped a question on whether he supports the anti-socialism resolution on Monday. "I haven't taken a look at that resolution, although it's my understanding that the resolution elevates the so-called SAVE America Act, which is just the 'Suppress the Vote Act.' And I'm not clear how many Democrats are actually gonna support a resolution whose focus is on trying to rig the midterm election by elevating this voter suppression legislation that Donald Trump has been trying to jam down the road to the American people for the last year," he told reporters. JOHNSON SCORES COMMANDING VICTORY IN FIGHT TO RAM SAVE AMERICA ACT THROUGH DEMOCRAT OPPOSITION In addition to condemning socialism, the resolution also hails Republican-led election security bills as "common-sense election integrity measures, including proof of citizenship, photo identification, and database checks." It calls for the "enforcement" of the Safeguarding American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, which has passed the House but has not been taken up in the Senate. Democrats have largely panned that legislation as attempts at voter suppression. Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon, D-Pa., said the bill was a bid to "silence political opponents." "Let's scare people with yet another boogeyman and not do anything about it. Not really solve problems, just try to scare people," Scanlon said. Meanwhile, Rep. Nick Langworthy, R-N.Y., pointed out that Democratic socialists were already in power in his own state and warned it could spread elsewhere. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I've seen firsthand the alarming rise of socialism...families in western New York have watched one-party rule in Albany pile on more taxes, more mandates, more government control, while hardworking taxpayers are left to foot the bill," Langworthy said. "And now downstate, we've watched the socialist left move more from the activist fringe into positions of real, serious political power. And anyone thinks that these ideas are going to stay confined in New York City is sadly mistaken."

news.title: Trump Voters Turn Away From President as Approval Rating Hits New Low
news.text: Some of President Donald Trump’s voters are turning away from him, as his approval rating reached a record low in the new University of Massachusetts Amherst poll released on Monday. Trump’s approval rating has major implications for the Republican Party in the midterms as it finds itself on the defensive in key races to control the House of Representatives and the Senate. The president’s popularity has waned since his return to office last year amid voter frustration over the economy, inflation and the unpopular war in Iran. Historically, when the president’s approval rating is low, his party loses seats in the midterms. Such was the case in 2018, when Republicans suffered losses in Trump’s first midterm. Democrats believe his approval slipping to new lows could allow them to expand the battleground into more traditionally conservative states like Texas. One in 6 Trump 2024 Voters Wouldn’t Vote for Him Again The new UMass poll found that 84 percent of Trump’s voters would vote for him again if the presidential election were held again, compared with about 94 percent of those who voted for Democratic former Vice President Kamala Harris, who said they would vote for her again. But many of those disaffected Trump voters would not necessarily cross parties to support Harris. Only 2 percent said they would vote for the former Democratic candidate, while 7 percent said they would vote for a third party and 7 percent simply would not vote at all if the election were held again. Among those who did not vote in 2024, only 20 percent said they would vote for Trump if the election were held again, compared to 27 percent who would vote for Harris and 14 percent who would vote for a third party. Forty percent would still not vote, the poll found. Meanwhile, Trump’s net approval rating fell to a new low of -32 points in the poll. Thirty-two percent of respondents said they approved of his job performance, while 64 percent disapproved. That’s a decline from a -29 point net approval in March 2026 and a -20 net approval rating in July 2025 in UMass Amherst polling. Tatishe Nteta, provost professor of political science at UMass Amherst and director of the poll, wrote in the memo that the “clock is ticking for President Trump and the Republican Party to offer solutions to the nation’s most pressing problems.” “A failure to do so will likely result not only in a continued decline in the President’s approval rating but could also put Republican control of the House of Representatives and possibly the U.S. Senate increasingly at risk,” he said. The poll surveyed 1,000 respondents from August 21 to 26, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. Donald Trump’s Approval Rating: What Other Polls Show The president’s approval rating has fallen in many polls as the midterms approach. A Morning Consult poll offered less of a grim picture for Republicans but still found him underwater at -14 points, 41 percent approving and 55 percent disapproving of the president’s job performance. It surveyed 2,203 registered voters from August 28 to 30, 2026, according to The New York Times. A Quantus Insights poll showed Trump's net approval at -15 points, with 42 percent approving and 57 percent disapproving. It surveyed 1,200 likely voters from August 26 to 28, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points. Trump’s approval stood at -21 points in the latest poll from YouGov and The Economist, which found 36 percent approving and 57 percent disapproving of his job performance. It surveyed 1,536 adults from August 21 to 24, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. Meanwhile, a Reuters/Ipsos poll showed his approval at -32 points, with 65 percent disapproving of Trump and 33 percent approving. The poll surveyed 1,215 adults from August 21 to 24, 2026. Trump Calls Out ‘Fake Polls’ Trump has criticized polls showing his approval rating has fallen in recent weeks. On August 30, the president hit back at polls in a post on Truth Social. “THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA ARE OUT OF CONTROL, AND SOMETHING MUST BE DONE ABOUT IT. FCC TO THE RESCUE! President DJT,” he wrote. A White House spokesperson pointed to that post when reached for comment by Newsweek. On August 24, he wrote that Democrats are “going CRAZY with Fake Polls.” “They’re putting them out at levels never seen before. They’re called, ‘Demoralization Operations,’ where they try to demoralize Republicans so that they don’t go out and vote — But the actual Polls are tremendous, and the Spirit in our Country has never been higher,” Trump wrote. Economy Behind Trump Approval Slump Trump’s approval rating decline comes as Americans remain dissatisfied with the economy. CNN data analyst Harry Enten said in a video posted to X on Monday that inflation was the “key reason” Trump was elected. He pointed to Ipsos polling showing that in August 2024, Trump was more trusted on inflation than Harris by 12 points among independents; in the latest polling, the president's approval on inflation among independents stood at -64 points. “You don’t see changes like this,” Enten said. “But the key issue that got him reelected, now he’s way down there in the Gulf of Mexico.” The UMass Amherst poll released on Monday found that only 22 percent of Americans believe Trump has handled inflation either very or somewhat well, while 75 percent said he has handled the matter not too well or not well at all. On jobs, 31 percent said he has handled the matter at least somewhat well, but 63 percent said he has handled it not too well or not well at all, according to the poll. The latest poll from YouGov and The Economist also showed growing dissatisfaction with the economy. It found that 39 percent of Americans trust Democrats more on the economy, while 32 percent trust Republicans more on the issue. Only 3 percent of respondents described the economy as in “excellent” condition, while 21 percent said it is in good condition. Thirty-three percent described the economy as fair, while 40 percent said it is poor. Americans were not optimistic about the economy's future, the poll found. Fifty-seven percent said it is getting worse, while 14 percent said it is getting better. Gas prices have also become a sticking point for the president, as they have surged during the Iran war due to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, a critical passageway for the global oil supply. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Sam Wilson.
news.summary: A new UMass poll found that 1 in 6 voters who cast their ballots for Trump in 2024 wouldn't vote for him again.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: Most ‘connected’ American Jews favor opposition win in Israel’s October election, survey finds
news.text: A majority of the “connected” US Jews surveyed would prefer Israel's current opposition to emerge victorious in the upcoming October elections, according to a new poll by the Jewish People Policy Institute published on Friday.The survey, which defined “connected” American Jews as “those with relatively strong ties to the Jewish community, Israel, and/or Jewish identity,” found that 54% of respondents had a “clear preference” for the current opposition.The next-largest group, 24%, said it was not their place to express a preference. Another 14% favored the current coalition, while 8% had no preference.While only 8% of respondents held Israeli citizenship and were eligible to vote, interest in the election was high among those polled, with 78% saying they followed election news either very or somewhat closely.“The strong interest of American Jews in elections in Israel demonstrates the importance of Israel to them, at least in two respects,” JPPI President Prof. Yedidia Stern told The Jerusalem Post.One of those reasons, Stern said, is that Israel's actions can shape how American Jews are perceived, meaning Israeli election results may have “practical implications for the status of Jews in the US.”The other, he said, is that Israel remains central to the identity of many American Jews. He added that JPPI surveys suggest the war has “strengthened Jewish identity” among a substantial segment of the community.Interest in the election was even higher among respondents eligible to vote in Israel.Among that group, 92% said they were following election coverage, including 63% who said they were following the upcoming election “very closely” and 29% who said they were following it “somewhat closely.”Survey panel of US Jews skews DemocraticThe survey primarily reflected the views of “connected” Jews, and the panel also had a Democratic majority. Sixty-two percent of respondents said they voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 US presidential election, while 30% said they voted for Donald Trump.The survey was not representative of all American Jews.Asked what that limitation might mean, Stern said it was reasonable to assume that Jews who are not connected to the community may not constitute a group particularly distinct from non-Jewish Americans as a whole.“However, I have no way of knowing whether this is indeed the case,” he added.Preferences in the Israeli election also closely tracked respondents' political orientations.Among those who identified as “strong conservatives,” only 8% preferred the opposition, while 56% favored the coalition. Among Trump voters, 43% favored the coalition.Support for the opposition rose steadily as respondents moved left politically: 21% among those who leaned conservative, 49% among centrists, 71% among those who leaned liberal, and 78% among those who identified as strong liberals.Just under three-quarters, or 74%, of Harris voters preferred an opposition victory.Among respondents outside the United States, 49% of Canadian respondents and 57% of UK respondents also said they preferred an opposition victory. JPPI cautioned, however, that the findings from those countries should be viewed as indicative because of their smaller sample sizes.Among US respondents eligible to vote in Israel, 55% preferred an opposition victory, more than double the 26% who favored the current coalition.
news.author: Sam Halpern

news.title: Stephen A Smith reveals Barack Obama privately called him after Biden criticism ahead of 2024 election
news.text: Podcast host Stephen A. Smith revealed on Friday that former President Barack Obama called him before the 2024 election to discuss his influence, noting that Obama wanted to speak privately rather than appear on his podcast. "What I never told y'all, and I never brought up, is that Barack Obama called me too. The content of that conversation will remain private because I will not violate trust," Smith said. "He called before the election to discuss my impact, but he didn't come on the podcast either." Smith spoke to "The Culture Table," hosted by Tori Cooper, Sumatra Abernathy and Ashley Christopher, about receiving a "thumbs-down" award from the National Association of Black Journalists (NABJ) at an Atlanta gala, defending himself against the criticism. STEPHEN A SMITH CALLS OUT JILL BIDEN, DEMS FOR 'LYING THROUGH THEIR TEETH' AND DAMAGING PARTY'S BRAND "It was after I said that we need a new president because Joe Biden clearly was done. You know, he clearly looked done. So the point is, folks like to talk to me privately, but then when I ask them to come on camera and to have a fruitful discussion, now they go elsewhere," he continued. "So it's like I'm taking these hits, and these are people that want to facilitate or assist in the facilitation of these narratives being disseminated and projected about me. But the same people calling me privately, having discussions upon which I have never violated. This is the first time anyone has ever heard me publicly state that Barack Obama called me," Smith said. OBAMA BLAMES SPLINTERED MEDIA FOR PREVENTING SUPERSTAR DEMOCRAT FROM RISING UP The former president's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Obama wasn't the only one Smith accused of not coming on his show. He also named former first lady Michelle Obama, former vice president Kamala Harris, Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. "I think the Democrats fear my footsteps," he said. "I think they know that they have a legitimate fear that I can influence the election potentially. I will never divulge what was said, but last week when I did my podcast and I responded to the NABJ, I pointed out how Kamala Harris reached out to me and asked to meet with me, and we met for two hours." KAMALA HARRIS BACKS MAJOR CHANGES TO THE SUPREME COURT, ELECTORAL COLLEGE AHEAD OF POSSIBLE 2028 CAMPAIGN "She did not speak to me and come on my show before the election," Smith said of Harris. "Once again, in my opinion, they take paths of smaller resistance." Harris' office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. AMERICA OWES BLACK WOMEN 'EVERYTHING,' REP JASMINE CROCKETT RANTS OVER JULY 4 WEEKEND Smith recently addressed the NABJ's thumbs-down award during his show. "The reality is that it was a personal hit job," Smith said. "We can sit up there and lollygag around and act like we don't know any better. It was a personal hit job. Which, by the way, usually doesn't phase me. I know you think something phases me, just because you see me commenting on it. No, I'm in this business. I have a platform. I can comment about anything I want to, and I will continue to do so." "That's not what this is," he added. "This is different. This is a journalism organization that didn't engage in journalism when it came to critiquing me. Disparaging Black women is a very incendiary thing to say. If you felt that adamant about it, [NABJ] President [Errin] Haines, how come I never got a call?" Smith speculated that the award was focused on his past criticism of high-profile Black female political figures like Crockett. He also revealed that he reached out to Haines regarding the organization's allegations to potentially discuss their differences, a conversation that ultimately went nowhere. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "While much of the public conversation in recent days has centered on Stephen A. Smith, he was one of five recipients named this year," the NABJ previously told Fox News Digital in a statement. "The concerns NABJ raised extend well beyond any one individual and include threats to editorial independence, the loss of newsroom diversity and reporting expertise, the treatment of Black journalists in the workplace, responsible use of influential media platforms, and decisions that affect the ability of journalists to fully and fairly cover Black communities and hold powerful institutions accountable." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News' Lindsay Kornick contributed to this report.
news.summary: Stephen A. Smith revealed Barack Obama called him before the 2024 election to discuss his impact, but would not appear on his podcast publicly.
news.author: Hanna Panreck

news.title: I Listened to The Diary of a CEO for a Week. This Is What It Did to Me
news.text:
There’s something unintentionally hilarious about The Diary of A CEO’s YouTube thumbnails. If you want to see how the modern attention economy works, have a look at them right now. The arrangement is always the same: the podcast’s host, Steven Bartlett, is on the right; the guest is on the left; and in the middle is a short, amped-up phrase to make you click. “AI Will Become A God By 2027!”; “It’s Simple To Lose Fat”; “Do Not Buy A House”; “We Have 4 Weeks Left.”
The best bits are the cut-outs of Bartlett himself, which cycle through about half a dozen shots of him in various poses of rapt concentration. In a couple, he’s concentrating so hard he’s put his index finger to his lips. In another, he has all four fingers resting there, as if his guest has stunned him into chewing off his own nails.
I wouldn’t usually have a reason to contemplate these pictures, but The Diary of a CEO is now too big to ignore, being the second-most-listened-to podcast on Spotify globally in 2025. JD Vance, Bruno Fernandes, Matthew McConaughey, Kamala Harris, and Kevin Hart are among the famous and powerful people Bartlett has sat down with between various scientists, self-help authors, and businesspeople.
And DOAC is now closing in on the juggernaut of the format, The Joe Rogan Experience—at least on YouTube. Bartlett got twice as many views there as Rogan between March and June this year, according to the analytics site Social Blade, and his growing subscriber base (currently 19.1 million) is on track to overtake Rogan’s relatively stagnant 21.1 million.
Millions, probably tens of millions, of people genuinely like Bartlett’s output. The last time he released demographic data on his audience, in 2023, the gender balance was almost perfectly even, but since then some of his episodes have had a whiff of the manosphere: one with podcaster and former Love Island star Chris Williamson, who partially blames the fertility crisis on some women having an “anti-family” attitude; another with the psychiatrist-turned-streamer Alok Kanojia, in which Bartlett asks if society should “put systems in place” to make sure single men meet partners. Is this pushing his audience towards inceldom? There was only one way to find out: spend a week DOAC-maxxing every opportunity I could.
I started on YouTube, where as mentioned, Bartlett really leans into his visuals. The episodes, released twice a week, have introductory montages animating the choice quotes. Below them is a banner asking me to “Shop the The Diary Of A CEO store,” which includes something called the “The 1% Diary,” a Bartlett-approved notebook with motivational quotes and a box to write in your “1% boost” for the day. It’s $41, and covers a “90-day journey,” so you’d need to drop $164 for not quite a year’s supply.
DOAC episodes are full of props, like the photos Bartlett slides across the table to his guests to elicit emotional anecdotes. When cancer researcher Thomas Seyfried appears as a guest, he waves around a brown envelope with “CONFIDENTIAL” written on it in cartoonishly large red letters, which contains an embargoed medical paper that’s pixelated when removed. This flair does not extend to Bartlett’s outfits, which seem to consist of an inexhaustible supply of black T-shirts.
The most popular interviews are an eclectic bunch, and don’t include any really famous guests: an AI expert on AI-proof jobs; a self-help author on “how to seduce anyone, build confidence and become powerful;” a neuroscientist on how stress “gives you belly fat.” Also a geopolitical analyst predicting World War Three. But as per its name, DOAC started with a focus on business—so as I’m brushing my teeth one evening, I open Spotify and throw on the episode with hedge fund billionaire Ray Dalio.
It’s interesting, not so much because of the content, which mostly consists of an introductory lesson in investing, but because Bartlett is never quite sure whether to position himself at his listeners’ level or at Dalio’s. He asks Dalio to explain basic finance jargon like “leverage” for the benefit of a general audience, but can’t resist hinting at his own connections to investors and startup founders. He does restrain himself from mentioning he’s a judge on Dragons’ Den (the UK's version of Shark Tank, which he will be a guest on in this upcoming season), at least before Dalio’s boomerish AI hyping lulls me gently to sleep.
Sometimes these attempted flexes go awry. “They call it a black swan event,” Bartlett says wisely when they’re discussing stock market bubbles popping. Do they? Black swan events are by definition surprises, and the one thing we know about bubbles is that they pop sooner or later. My favorite Bartlettism: when interviewing computer scientist Roman Yampolskiy, at one point he asks, “You’re the founder of the term ‘AI safety’?” Words aren’t companies, Stevie.
I leap to DOAC’s other pillar: wellness. The show has previously been criticized for platforming, and not challenging, fringe medical views. Early last year it started fact-checking episodes with a medical doctor; “DOAC community notes” occasionally pop up on screen to correct, clarify or offer context to what guests are saying. But misinformation only makes an impact if listeners actually pay attention to it—and given most episodes are more than 90 minutes long and sometimes run for two and a half hours, I’m not convinced this is always the case. For all its hyper-clicky thumbnails and opening montages, DOAC also exploits our desire for infinite, ambient content we can sort-of-consume while going about our days. It works for viral TikTok clips, and for background noise.
Bartlett’s husky vocal fry has an ASMR quality to it; he has a habit of repeating back what his guest has just said, like a slightly confused hypnotist. Is he hypnotizing me? I can’t help but be a little entranced on a drowsy commute into work, while listening to an episode on how vitamins affect sleep. Though it’s bookended by the key points, the rest of it is rambling. It’s less of an interrogation than Bartlett periodically prompting his guest to keep talking.
But for emotional matters, Bartlett sits up in his chair and gets his scalpel out. It’s something of a meme how often guests cry on DOAC, to the point where there’s literally a TikTok discover page called “Steven Bartlett Making Guests Cry” —mostly about bereavements, but also Jordan Peterson tearing up about the music of Hank Williams.
Bartlett begins his assault on Vice President J.D. Vance’s tear ducts by sliding him some of those family photos. He locks onto the vice president’s mom. “What would she think of you today? What would you say to her? Have you ever grieved [her] loss?” Vance wells up. “The emotion’s still right on the surface for you,” Bartlett says, as if his last half-dozen questions haven’t been bulldozing their way through Vance’s outward composure. At another point, Vance is talking about his chaotic early relationship with his now wife, which Bartlett says is “clearly an avoidant attachment style.” “100%,” Vance replies—this trad Cath, anti-woke warrior is now lapping up psychology speak.
That’s prime SB, greasing all his guests, however varied, into a DOAC-shaped box, so consumers can get the product they know and love week after week. “I meet so many different people, and one of the things I’ve come to learn is [to] try and meet everybody as I experience them,” he says to Vance at one point. Though Bartlett doesn’t particularly challenge his guests, he steers episodes so we always end up getting a lot of him in them—a lot of emotion, speculation, sensationalism and meandering.
I end my DOAC journey in the most appropriate way I can think of: listening to an episode titled “Top Scientist REVEALS: We Invented Heaven, God Is A Human Invention!” at 1.5x speed. Near the end of the two hours, theoretical physicist Brian Greene has just about finished running us through the eventual heat death of the universe when Bartlett asks him if there’s any aspect of his work that might be relevant to his listeners’ day-to-day lives. There isn’t—he’s a theoretical physicist.
But after a week of sustaining myself on a heavy diet of Steven Bartlett, I’ve started to absorb the malign philosophy that seems to hang in the background of his interviews: that all knowledge, however niche, should be valued on whether it can make you more fulfilled and successful. And some of the knowledge is quite niche. It’s been suggested that I shouldn’t buy a house, but maybe Bitcoin instead; that I should spend more time outdoors in the sun (fair enough) and consider applying a bit less sunscreen when I do (hmmm); that a keto diet could help cancer treatments like chemotherapy (what?); that “they” (who are they?) are lying to me about AI, and about UFOs; and that according to an “ex-Google officer” I only have three years left “before it hits.” What is “it?” Correct! It’s AI taking your job, unless you listen to this 122-minute podcast.
I feel simultaneously more amped up and twitchy, given all the essential views and theories DOAC is pitching to me, but also less focused—more smooth-brained—given how long and rambling the episodes are. I don’t feel particularly “radicalized,” really; in relation to AI and wellness, politics is just a fraction of Bartlett’s output, of which anything that could be called vaguely manosphere-y is a further fraction.
And what I definitely don’t feel is optimized. But the content itself isn’t optimized. It isn’t cool-headed and concise, but as brash and bottomless as the internet at large. DOAC might say success is about discipline, but its own success comes from the very modern tactic of simply flooding the zone.
A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.
news.summary: Steven Bartlett’s podcast is on track to become the biggest in the world. Can it help me self-optimize to happiness?
news.author: Josiah Gogarty

news.title: Neither Democrats Nor Republicans Have Won Over the Working Class. A New Poll Shows Deep Distrust of Both Parties.
news.text: Working-class voters have become one of the most fiercely contested groups in American politics, but a new survey suggests neither Republicans nor Democrats have convinced them that their promises are genuine.According to new results from The POLITICO Poll, 55% of Americans believe politicians who say they want to help the working class are primarily trying to win votes. The skepticism crosses political lines, with majorities of voters who backed President Donald Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris sharing that view.Among Americans who identify as working class, only one in four believe politicians genuinely want to help people like them. The findings show the challenge facing both parties ahead of the November midterm elections, when control of Congress will be at stake, and economic concerns are expected to play a central role.Neither party has established a decisive advantage with working-class Americans. The poll found 38% of those voters believe Democrats best represent their interests, compared with 32% who chose Republicans. Among Americans overall, 37% said Democrats better represent the working class, while 30% favored Republicans.For Democrats, those numbers come amid an internal debate over how to reconnect with voters who have moved toward the GOP as the Democratic coalition has become increasingly reliant on college-educated Americans."We've struggled with the working class for quite a while and it's been a combination of being out of touch with working class values on a lot of culture issues and being seen as either not helpful or not helpful enough on economic issues," Jim Kessler, executive vice president for policy at the centrist Democratic think tank Third Way, told the outlet.Progressives argue their economic agenda offers a stronger route back. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., told POLITICO that progressives are "speaking to the needs of working families," pointing to issues including universal health care.Republicans face a different problem: preserving the working-class gains Trump made in the 2024 election, particularly among Black and Latino voters who were frustrated by the economy under former President Joe Biden.The poll also highlights how difficult it is to define the constituency both parties are trying to win. When respondents were simply asked whether "working class" described them, 59% said yes and 31% said no. But when asked to choose among labels including wealthy, middle class, lower middle class, working class and poor, just 16% selected working class.That discrepancy suggests "working class" functions as something broader than a traditional income category for many Americans, potentially encompassing people who depend on a paycheck regardless of occupation or education.The economic picture could create particular challenges for Republicans. According to the POLITICO survey, 35% of self-identified working-class Americans said Trump is fully responsible for the current economy. Half said the president has spent too much time focused on international affairs rather than domestic issues, while many said the ongoing war in Iran has made life more expensive.Both parties are already trying to demonstrate working-class credentials ahead of November. Vice President JD Vance recently returned to Middletown, Ohio, and spoke at the steel plant where his grandfather worked. In Georgia, Republican Senate nominee Rep. Mike Collins frequently highlights his background as a trucker.Democrats are similarly fielding candidates with blue-collar biographies, including union leader and former smokejumper Sam Forstag in Montana and firefighter union chief Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania.
news.author: Matias Civita

news.title: Trump official blasts ‘name-calling’ by Canada - despite it being the president’s go-to attack
news.text:
A senior Treasury official on Monday condemned "name-calling" in politics following critical remarks from Canadian leaders, glossing over President Donald Trump's long track record of using personal insults against his political opponents.

Under Secretary for International Affairs Erin Browne addressed the diplomatic friction while appearing on "NewsNation," speaking from the G20 Summit in Asheville, North Carolina.

The interview turned to recent remarks by Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who had previously called Trump a "dictator" and a "bully," even as Ford urged calm and noted that the U.S. and Canada remain "allies" and "best friends."

When asked by anchor Markie Martin how heavily the trade dispute with Ottawa would affect the summit, Browne pushed back against the rhetoric.

news.title: Lawmakers Slam Far-Right Laura Loomer's Racist Rants Against Angie Nixon
news.text:
An increasing number of lawmakers are ripping self-described white nationalist Laura Loomer for her latest racist remarks against several Black women in politics — including Florida’s progressive Senate candidate Angie Nixon, whom she called a “ghetto bitch.”

Loomer received a wave of backlash after calling powerful Black women like Nixon, Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), former Rep. Cori Bush (D-Mo.) and Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson “ghetto, entitled, race-obsessed, destructive black bitches.” Nixon responded to Loomer, only for the “proud Islamophobe” to triple down on her comments.

“You attack and insult Black women because you believe peddling racism is good for your clicks and your business model,” Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) posted on X. “And while everyone with internet access and ignorant opinions doesn’t deserve a response, this is someone who is an advisor of Donald Trump and who should be condemned by all.”

Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) called out the fact that the vast majority of Democrats, including top leaders, have yet to publicly condemn the remarks as of Monday morning.

“To all who have attacked Hasan Piker, I’m going to check to see if you said anything about Laura Loomer calling a Black woman running for Senate in Florida, Representative Angie Nixon, a ghetto b**** and said that she should tug on her leash,” the congresswoman posted on social media, referring to the leftist figure who has become the target of centrist Democrats.

Notably, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, who herself was embroiled in racist scandals before breaking from President Donald Trump’s MAGA agenda, beat most major Democrats and the rest of the Republican Party in publicly denouncing the influential right-winger’s comments against Nixon, who is running against Sen. Ashley Moody (R).

“I’m not a Democrat and I’m not supporting Angie Nixon, but the Republican Party and President Trump owns Laura Loomer and her nonstop vitriol. This hateful, racists [sic], and demeaning rhetoric should not be tolerated. Ever,” she posted on X. “But they allow it and keep her in the inner circle.”

“Loomer hurts Republican Senator Ashley Moody in her race with these vicious attacks. Just like Loomer has consistently hurt the Republican Party as she whispers nonstop insanity in the President’s ear,” Greene continued. “I 1000% denounce Laura Loomer and her nasty, hateful, racists [sic] comments. This is Trump’s new MAGA and Republican Party and I want nothing to do with it.”

A spokesperson for Moody’s campaign did not immediately respond to HuffPost’s request for comment, though Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.) has demanded the senator condemn Loomer’s remarks.

This weekend wasn’t the first time Loomer made racist statements against Black women in politics. The Trump adviser faced heat last year after saying Rep. Jasmine Crockett’s reported treatment of her staff is “typical DEI Shaniqua behavior.” In 2024, Loomer said the White House would “smell like curry” if former Vice President Kamala Harris, who is also South Asian, won the presidential election.

Loomer’s latest comments come just days after a grand jury report found Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis’ (R) administration — of which Moody served as attorney general — had “misappropriated” $10 million in taxpayer dollars from a children’s nonprofit to the Republican Party of Florida.

In its report, the grand jury specifically criticized Moody for failing to ensure taxpayer money wasn’t being misspent. DeSantis appointed Moody to the U.S. Senate four months after the transfer.

“While Loomer throws racist tantrums, my opponent, unelected Senator Ashley Moody, continues to hide after a grand jury confirmed she knowingly allowed $10 million meant for sick, needy children to be stolen for a political slush fund,” Nixon said in a Monday statement. “Moody has broken the public trust and should resign immediately.”

news.title: James Clyburn says supporting Clarence Thomas for supreme court ‘was mistake’
news.text:
The senior Democratic congressman James Clyburn said his decision to support Clarence Thomas for a US supreme court seat “was a mistake” and called for the expansion of the nation’s highest legal panel to 13 justices.

Clyburn, of South Carolina, spoke up for Thomas at his fiery 1991 confirmation hearings, calling him “a personal and professional friend” who would use their shared experiences lifting minorities and advancing civil rights to become a respected and accomplished jurist.

Instead, Clyburn told NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, Thomas abandoned his principles to become an extremist, hard-right member of a bench that has delivered some stunning legal reversals in recent years, including the overturning of federal protections for abortion and ending affirmative action in higher education.

Asked by host Kristen Welker if he regretted standing up for Thomas, Clyburn replied: “I have made mistakes in my life, and that’s one that I made. And I will own up to that mistake.

“I had no idea that Clarence Thomas would rebel the way he has against his own background and experiences. He was raised by his grandfather, and he has shown very little sensitivity to the environment his grandfather grew up down in Pin Point, Georgia.”

Before joining Congress in 1993, Clyburn was South Carolina’s human affairs commissioner for 18 years beginning in 1974. He said Thomas’s tenure as chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission from 1982 until 1990, a time in which it vigorously pursued anti-discrimination legal actions, had assured him that Thomas “believed in precedents, the law”.

He told Welker: “I had faith and confidence in the fact that his background and experiences would instruct him in his professionalism, especially sitting on the bench. I thought, sure, that he would be here upholding those precedents set down in 1954 in the Brown v Board of Education decision” that declared racial segregation in public schools was illegal.

But Thomas, whose later years on the bench have been mired in allegations of corruption, turned his back on civil rights, Clyburn suggested, notably in the 2024 decision on ideological grounds that ruled affirmative action in college admissions unconstitutional.

“That was a mistake on my part,” Clyburn said of his past support for Thomas. “And I own up to it.”

Clyburn spoke as the prospect of increasing the number of US supreme court justices, a popular rallying cry for sections of the Democratic party as it attempts to retake the House in November’s midterms, returned to public discourse.

Former Democratic vice-president Kamala Harris in July called for the expansion of the bench from nine to 13, a proposal Clyburn said he would support.

“Thirteen is a pretty good number,” he said. “A baker’s dozen would be a good number to have on the court.

“And I would hope we would get people on the court who will follow the constitutional underpinnings of this great nation of ours. I had hoped that Clarence Thomas would follow the underpinnings of that constitution of ours, but he has not done so.

“In fact, he’s decided to go all the way from an angry leftist, to a very angry rightist.”

Clyburn, however, said Democrats’ immediate priorities after November should not be either supreme court expansion or impeachment of Donald Trump for what would be a third time across his two presidencies.

“If the Democrats were to take back the House, and I feel confident that we will, our first order of business ought to be developing an accessible and affordable campaign effort that will yield what I will call making this country, its greatness, accessible and affordable for all of its citizens,” he said.

news.title: Seth Moulton's Chances of Defeating 80-Year-Old Ed Markey: Final Polls
news.text: Senator Ed Markey holds a substantial polling lead over Representative Seth Moulton ahead of the Democratic primary in the Massachusetts Senate race, defying a trend of generational change that has defined this year's primaries. Moulton, 47, has cast himself as part of a new generation of Democratic leaders in his bid against Markey, an 80-year-old who first entered Congress in 1976. Moulton has sought to make the case for new leadership in the Senate against a longtime incumbent, as many Democrats have grown frustrated with their party’s aging representation in Washington. The primary challenge by Moulton comes as an anti-incumbent wave has swept through this year’s Democratic primaries, and several longtime incumbents have lost to political newcomers. In addition to age, many incumbents have also lost to more progressive challengers or democratic socialists. But Massachusetts has different ideological dynamics at play. Markey has positioned himself as one of the most progressive senators, touting his support for Medicare for All and the Green New Deal, while Moulton is viewed as more moderate. Moulton, who represents a district based around the North Shore, has criticized his party’s position on transgender rights and has declined to support Medicare for All. The primary will gauge whether Democrats in a solidly liberal state are willing to ditch a longtime senator whose age has drawn scrutiny, even when the challenger is not as progressive. Suffolk University Political Research Center Director David Paleologos told Newsweek he believes Markey has a substantial advantage heading into the primary. “When we released our final poll three weeks ago, I stated that this race was never close in the polling and that Markey had locked up the demographics he needed to win. I stand by that statement today,” Paleologos said. Newsweek reached out to the Markey campaign via press contact form and the Moulton campaign via email for comment. Ed Markey vs. Seth Moulton: What the Polls Show The latest polling shows Markey with a comfortable lead over Moulton. Markey led the latest Emerson College poll by 31 points, 60 percent to 33 percent. It surveyed 550 likely voters from August 28 to 29, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.1 percentage points. It marks a surge in Markey’s support compared to May, when he led an Emerson poll by only 5 points, 37 percent to 32 percent, suggesting previously undecided voters have backed the incumbent. Only 7 percent of voters were undecided in the new poll, down from 29 percent in May. A poll from the University of Massachusetts Amherst similarly showed Markey leading Moulton. It showed Markey with support from 60 percent of respondents compared to Moulton’s 32 percent. It surveyed 445 self-identified Democratic primary voters from August 5 to 12, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 5.8 percentage points among Democratic voters. Among Democrats, 82 percent of respondents approved of the incumbent Democratic senator's job performance. A poll from Suffolk University and The Boston Globe showed Markey up nearly 15 points, 52.2 percent to 37.6 percent. It surveyed 500 Massachusetts residents from August 13 to 16, 2026. Paleologos told Newsweek that Markey’s big win among key demographics, including women, registered Democrats, progressive voters, Suffolk County residents and those who have already voted, has helped him build a polling lead. Markey is also favored in prediction markets; Kalshi gave him a 98.7 percent chance of winning on Monday, while his likelihood of victory stood at 99 percent on Polymarket. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment in the moment but do not always predict the future accurately. Why Ed Markey Could Defy Generational Challenge While calls for generational change have become a major issue in the midterms, policy and ideology remain an important factor for primary voters. Markey’s progressive bona fides may be helping him build support among the more liberal wing of the Democratic primary. Paleologos said Moulton “needed to triangulate” the arguments around age, that Markey wouldn’t be able to lead the progressive agenda if reelected and his arguments around his own vision as a senator. “He was only able to do the first, and the political tripod doesn't stand on one leg,” he said. UMass political scientists Tatishe Nteta, Jesse Rhodes, Jesse Usher Barrett, and Sydney Brake wrote in a Substack post breaking down their latest poll on Monday that Markey’s popularity, progressive bona fides and support for transgender rights have bolstered his campaign. “The average Democratic primary voter is even further to the left than the average Massachusetts voter, and these voters prefer a progressive candidate,” they wrote. “This is good news for Markey, whom likely Democratic primary voters view as the more progressive candidate.” Moulton, who garnered national attention for his 2020 presidential run, has also faced scrutiny from some Democrats over his past remarks about transgender athletes, an issue that has divided the party. In an interview with The New York Times last year, Moulton said, “I have two little girls. I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete.” Markey is no stranger to facing a competitive primary. In 2020, then-Representative Joe Kennedy III challenged Markey, making similar arguments around the need for generational change. But Markey won that race by nearly 10 points. He did so by unifying more progressive voters in the solidly blue state. He also won support among younger Democrats, who helped build his social media presence on the “Markeyverse,” a network of meme accounts that supported his reelection. Notably, Markey is not the only older progressive leader. In neighboring Vermont, 84-year-old Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, is one of the country's most prominent progressives and won reelection in 2024. Still, age has become a sore spot for the Democratic Party, particularly after former President Joe Biden had a disastrous debate against President Donald Trump in 2024. The debate, which came after Biden opted to run for a second term despite age concerns voiced both outside and within the party, was seen as a major turning point in Trump's reelection that culminated in Biden's exit from the race. When Is the Massachusetts Primary Election? The Massachusetts primary election is set for September 1, 2026. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., according to the Secretary of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts' office. Who Is Republican John Deaton? Can He Flip Massachusetts? John Deaton, an attorney, is viewed as the presumptive Republican nominee in the Senate race. He was the party’s nominee in the 2024 race against Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, losing by nearly 20 points. The general election is not expected to be competitive, as Massachusetts has long been viewed as one of the bluest states in the country. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won Massachusetts in 2024 by 25 points over Trump. In 2020, it backed Biden by more than 33 points. Boston is a Democratic powerhouse that often elects some of the country's most progressive lawmakers, and the rest of the state, including more rural areas out west, is also quite blue. Trump did not win a single county in the state in any of his three presidential runs. A poll from UMass Amherst showed both Markey and Moulton ahead of Deaton. Markey led by 21 points, 51 percent to 30 percent, while Moulton led by 24 points, 49 percent to 25 percent. Paleologos said he doesn’t believe the race will become competitive “because Donald Trump will still be the president for two more years.” “Even if Markey has a senior moment in a bad debate, he'd still probably win,” he said. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Sam Wilson.
news.summary: Moulton says it's time for new Democratic leadership. Are Massachusetts voters ready to pick him over their longtime senator?

news.title: Kamala Harris endorses Chris Pappas in New Hampshire Senate race
news.text:
Pappas, considered the best-known candidate in the Democratic primary, has received numerous endorsements from labor unions and abortion-rights groups in the Granite State. Now, he is adding Harris to that list.

The New Hampshire Senate race is the latest contest to receive an endorsement from the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee. Besides Pappas, Harris is also backing Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) in his reelection bid and Michigan Senate Democratic nominee Abdul el Sayed.

Other Democratic candidates, however, are intentionally distancing themselves from the former vice president.

Mary Peltola, who is running for the Senate in Alaska, recently rejected an unsolicited fundraising email sent by Harris’s Fight for the People PAC. Last week, Josh Turek, who is running for the Senate in Iowa, said Harris should not be campaigning for him. Iowa Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand made a similar statement to Turek.

Harris has frequently waded into politics during the midterm elections as she considers mounting a 2028 presidential campaign.

Her endorsement of Pappas is expected to carry some weight in New Hampshire, given that she won the state by nearly 3 points over President Donald Trump in 2024.

In New Hampshire’s Sept. 8 primary, Pappas will face a challenge from socialist Karishma Manzur for the party’s nomination. Pappas leads the rest of the primary field, with Manzur 13 points behind him in a recent poll from the University of New Hampshire.

SOCIALIST SURGE THREATENS DEMOCRATS IN NEW HAMPSHIRE SENATE RACE

On the Republican side, Scott Brown and John Sununu are among the top candidates. Brown once represented Massachusetts in the Senate before moving to New Hampshire, where he ran against Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH) in 2014. Sununu, who is endorsed by Trump, previously served in the New Hampshire Senate.

Shaheen is retiring at the end of her third term early next year, leaving her seat open for the first time since 2009.

Chris Pappas (D-NH) on Monday as he prepares to face other Democratic primary challengers running for an open Senate seat in New Hampshire. “@KamalaHarris has stood tall for democracy and is committed to making this country fairer and freer for all,” Pappas wrote on X. news.title: Trump Faces Backlash From Critics Over 'Gross' Move With Natalie Harp as Wife Melania Is Nowhere in Sight
news.text:
Donald Trump is facing renewed backlash after being seen in another close situation with his much younger blonde aide, Natalie Harp, RadarOnline.com can report.

The president and his assistant were spotted together on a golf course, while Trump's wife, Melania, was nowhere in sight.Critics Call Out Natalie Harp and Donald Trump's 'Closeness'A photo on X showed Trump, 80, and Harp, 35, seated inside a car at his golf course in Virginia over the weekend. Harp accompanied the president on his trip and was caught flashing a wide smile while looking down at her phone as she sat next to him. 

But her proximity to the prez raised red flags online, and many critics have questioned their bond.

"What is wrong him, and HER?? That whole situation is so gross," one person posted on X, as another echoed, "He is a pathetic mess. And she is worse."

A third person exclaimed, "GROSS! I get the ew gross ick shivers just thinking about being in a confined space with that man. H-ll no." 

Another critic asked, "Why does she always have that creepy smile?"Natalie Harp's Role in Donald Trump's Social Media AccountsHarp's smile has been called out at Trump events in the past. Just last week, she was accused of "staring and smiling" in a video posted to X while the president's voice was heard on a speakerphone addressing a crowd of people.

The loyal aide also came under heavy fire regarding her role in crafting Trump's "personal" Truth Social posts.

A clip from the 2024 Apple TV documentary The Art of the Surge recently went viral, showing Harp typing out Trump's social media posts as he watched then-Vice President Kamala Harris' 2024 convention speech.

The video led to speculation about whether Harp personally types all of the president's posts and whether she is responsible for his constant spelling and grammatical errors.Melania Trump Comes Back Into the SpotlightMeanwhile, the more Harp is seen at the president's side, the more questions are raised about where First Lady Melania is. After not being seen in roughly a month, the 56-year-old finally made a public appearance on August 20 to announce a new initiative for foster care youth.

Melania strode into the White House Rose Garden with her hand tightly clenched to Donald's in a supposed show of unity.

She began her remarks by addressing her absence, snagging a few laughs when she said, "I heard you missed me. Here I am."Melania Trump's Timing Is QuestionedSkeptics, however, found the timing of Melania's reappearance suspect, especially given Harp's increased access to her husband.

"As soon as Natalie starts grabbing headlines, all of a sudden Melania's back in the spotlight," one person commented. "Surely, just a coincidence!"

Another person claimed, "We all knew that after the pearl-clutching about Dumpy's 'Binky' (aka Harp), the inevitable 'proof of life' photo op of Melania happens. They're so frkn obvious, it's astounding."
news.summary: Donald Trump and Natalie Harp were spotted on a golf course in Virginia, while his wife, Melania, was nowhere to be seen.

news.title: 'Whoa!' Bottom drops out for Trump as decisive midterm voting bloc flees in droves
news.text:
The decisive voter bloc in this year's midterm elections has dramatically shifted away from President Donald Trump and the Republican Party on the issue that helped elect him, according to CNN's Harry Enten.

In August 2024, independents trusted Trump over then-Vice President Kamala Harris on inflation by 12 percentage points, a margin Enten described as a key factor in Trump's victory. That advantage has since collapsed, and Trump's net approval rating on inflation among independents now stands at 64 points underwater – marking a swing of 76 points in a little over two years.

"Whoa!" Enten said. "You don't see changes like this. But the key issue that got him elected, now he's way down there in the Gulf of Mexico."

A similar reversal has occurred at the party level. In August 2022, ahead of that year's midterms, independents trusted Republicans over Democrats on inflation by 27 points, a margin that helped the GOP retake the House, but independents now say they trust Democrats more on the issue, by 18 points — a 45-point swing from four years ago.

Enten said such large shifts in voter trust on a single issue are unusual, and noted that the change matters because inflation remains the top concern for independent voters heading into November.

According to the data presented, 38 percent of independents named inflation as their top issue, followed by 14 percent who cited the broader economy and 10 percent who pointed to the conflict with Iran, which Enten said is also closely tied to economic concerns. Combined, more than half of independents identified inflation or the economy as their most pressing issue.

Gas prices, a visible driver of inflation concerns, may not offer Republicans relief before Election Day.

Enten said the combination of persistently high gas prices and the sharp erosion of trust on inflation, the very issue that fueled Republican gains in both the 2022 and 2024 elections, could pose a significant risk for the party in this year's midterm contests, given how central the issue clearly remains to independent voters' concerns.
